paragraphs.heading: What electromagnetism is
paragraphs.text: Electromagnetism is the interaction between particles that carry electric charge, acting through electromagnetic fields. It is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It is also the main force at work when atoms and molecules interact. It ties together three closely linked things: electricity, magnetism and optics.

paragraphs.heading: The glue of everyday matter
paragraphs.text: The electrostatic pull between an atom's nucleus and its electrons is what holds the atom together. Electric forces also let different atoms join into molecules. The force is behind many chemical and physical events in daily life. Even when you push or pull an ordinary object, the force you feel comes from forces between the molecules in your body and those in the object.

paragraphs.heading: Fields and waves
paragraphs.text: Physicists describe electromagnetism with fields. A field gives the electric and magnetic influence at each place and moment. At any point, the electromagnetic field is a mix of an electric field and a magnetic field. Because the two are linked, a disturbance in the electric field stirs the magnetic field, which in turn stirs the electric field again. The result is an oscillation that travels through space, called an electromagnetic wave.

paragraphs.heading: From lightning to light
paragraphs.text: People have studied it since ancient times, trying to explain lightning, static electricity, and the pull between magnetized iron ore and compasses. In the 18th and 19th centuries scientists worked out the mathematics linking these effects to electric charges and currents. They also showed that electricity and magnetism are related and can produce waves that keep themselves going. Those waves make up visible light and every other kind of electromagnetic radiation, from gamma rays and x-rays to microwaves and radio waves.

paragraphs.heading: Relativity and photons
paragraphs.text: Scientists keep refining the theory to fit modern physics, including quantum mechanics and relativity. Two of its consequences helped inspire Einstein's special relativity in 1905: observations must agree when seen from frames of reference moving in different ways, and the speed of light is set by properties of the medium it travels through. Quantum electrodynamics, or QED, adjusts Maxwell's equations to fit the quantized nature of matter. In QED, changes in the field come as separate packets called photons, the quanta of light.

paragraphs.heading: Strength and reach
paragraphs.text: Of the four fundamental forces, electromagnetism is the second strongest, and its range has no limit. Everyday forces such as friction and contact forces are not fundamental; they come from the four basic ones. At high energy, electromagnetism and the weak force merge into a single interaction, called the electroweak interaction.

paragraphs.heading: Inside modern technology
paragraphs.text: Electromagnetism plays key roles across modern technology. It underlies making, converting and delivering electrical energy, and producing and detecting light, heat and sound. Fiber optic and wireless communication depend on it. So do sensors, computing, electrolysis, electroplating, and the motors and actuators that make machines move.
